title: Canonical direct rotation
subtitle: G2 lecture 049000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: Suppose someone hands us two lines in the plane.
body: We can rotate the first line onto the second. But even there, the instruction does not specify a unique answer. We might turn through the smaller angle, turn the other way through a larger angle, or first rotate and then reflect along a suitable direction. For two subspaces of a Hilbert space, this freedom is much larger. We can move vectors within the source subspace, and within its orthogonal complement, while still sending the source subspace onto the target. A particular unitary transport can be constructed from the two orthogonal projections.

slides.title: Begin with the planar picture
slides.lead: Let U be the horizontal line and V be the line tilted counterclockwise by theta degrees, with theta strictly between zero and ninety degrees.
body: There is an ordinary rotation through theta. There is also a rotation through theta plus one hundred eighty degrees. Both carry U onto V, because a line has no preferred orientation. But the second motion sends a horizontal unit vector to the negative of the nearest unit vector along V. That difference appears in an inner product. The smaller rotation moves a horizontal unit vector to a vector whose inner product with it is cosine theta, which is positive. The larger one gives negative cosine theta. So positivity can help choose between transports.

slides.title: Reassemble the two projections
slides.lead: Write P for projection onto U and Q for projection onto V.
body: A natural transport candidate K is the sum of Q P and the product of identity minus Q with identity minus P. It sends the U component toward V and the U-perpendicular component toward V perpendicular. Its squared modulus is identity minus the square of P minus Q. Let C be the positive square root of that squared modulus. On a principal plane with angle theta, C multiplies each vector by cosine theta. So K acts there like cosine theta times an ordinary rotation. If the operator gap between P and Q is strictly below one, C has a bounded inverse. Then the direct rotation W is K times C inverse.

slides.title: Acuteness is weaker than a uniform gap
slides.lead: Call a pair acute in the intersection sense when neither subspace contains a nonzero vector perpendicular to the other.
body: More precisely, U intersect V perpendicular is zero, and U perpendicular intersect V is zero. For finite-dimensional pairs, this rules out right-angle principal vectors and gives a positive smallest cosine. In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, every individual principal angle may be strictly less than ninety degrees while a sequence approaches ninety degrees. The cosine then has no kernel, yet its inverse is unbounded. We must not confuse these two hypotheses. A projection gap strictly below one implies the intersection-based condition.

slides.title: How do we recognize the correct unitary?
slides.lead: Suppose T is any unitary that intertwines P and Q.
body: The intertwining identity says T P equals Q T. Consequently T carries U onto V and also carries U perpendicular onto V perpendicular. That alone allows too much freedom. We need a test involving the directions in which T moves the source decomposition. Compress T back to U: project onto U, apply T, and project onto U again. Do the analogous operation on U perpendicular. These are called the two diagonal compressions of T. For the canonical polar factor W, both diagonal compressions are positive operators. Positive means self-adjoint and having nonnegative quadratic form.

slides.title: Prove uniqueness instead of guessing it
slides.lead: Let T be a unitary intertwiner whose two diagonal compressions are positive.
body: We want to show T equals W when the crossed defects vanish. Define B to be the sum of those two diagonal compressions. Since each is positive, B is positive. And since both are supported in orthogonal pieces, B is block diagonal relative to U and U perpendicular. The projection intertwining identity lets us rewrite our original operator K as T times B. To see the structure, recall that Q equals T P T adjoint. Substitute that identity into both terms defining K. The two terms become T times the two diagonal blocks of T adjoint.

slides.title: A square made from two reflections
slides.lead: Every orthogonal projection determines a reflection.
body: Reflect through U by leaving U fixed and reversing U perpendicular. As an operator, this is twice P minus the identity. Define the corresponding reflection through V using Q. On our principal plane, reflecting through U and then reflecting through V is a rotation through twice theta. This is a familiar geometry theorem, and we can now understand it operatorially. Let J U be reflection through U and J V reflection through V. Their product, in that order, is the unitary operator J V after J U. The canonical direct rotation W is the half-angle motion, so on every principal plane W squared equals J V times J U.

slides.title: Reversing the direction
slides.lead: A good transport construction should behave predictably when we interchange the source and target.
body: Rotate from U to V, then rotate back from V to U. Those two motions ought to undo each other. Indeed, swapping P and Q replaces K by K adjoint. The positive polar factors are consequently adjoints of one another. So the canonical direct rotation from V to U is W adjoint, which equals W inverse because W is unitary. The same observation explains why the squared reflection product reverses. Its adjoint is J U followed by J V, precisely the reflection product for the reversed pair.

slides.title: Reconstruction
slides.lead: There are four things to prove for yourself.
body: First, calculate the polar modulus of K and show it is the positive cosine operator. Second, explain why vanishing crossed defects makes the polar factor unitary even when cosine has no bounded inverse. Third, prove uniqueness: an intertwining unitary with positive diagonal blocks factors K as that unitary times a positive block-diagonal operator. Identify the latter with the modulus of K. Fourth, verify on an actual plane that two reflections give twice the angle, and explain why the principal half-angle branch fails at minus one.
